en.title: Arabic: the whole course
en.short: What the Arabic degree covers, how it is organised, its main areas and how to study them.
keywords: teaching arabic as a foreign language

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Arabic is a Semitic language and the language of the Qur’an. This course studies the language itself (its sounds, script, word building and grammar), the literature written in it, and the culture of the peoples who use it. It is not only a language course. You also learn how Arabic has been described by its own scholars, how it varies across regions, and how it is translated, taught and processed by computers.

Arabic is unusual among world languages in one respect: a very old written form, often called Classical Arabic, still sits close to the modern written standard. Most writing and formal speech today uses Modern Standard Arabic, while everyday speech uses regional dialects. Much of the course is about holding those two facts together.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degrees differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook for the rules that bind you. Common titles are BA Arabic, BA Arabic Studies, and combined degrees such as Arabic with Islamic Studies, Arabic with French, or Arabic and Linguistics.

In Nigeria, a bachelor’s degree is usually four years, with the first year spent on language foundations and later years on literature, linguistics and a project. Arabic is also studied inside Arabic and Islamic Studies departments. In many Arab countries the bachelor’s degree is commonly four years as well, but the balance between language, literature and religious sciences varies. Some universities elsewhere teach Arabic within Middle Eastern or Asian studies.

A master’s degree usually adds a taught component and a dissertation. Coursework, credit hours, grading and award classifications are set locally.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The intro stage builds the base. You start with the script and phonology: the letters, their forms, the short vowels and other marks, and the sounds. Then morphology (sarf), how words are built from roots and patterns, and grammar (nahw), how sentences are made. Reading and comprehension, writing and composition, and oral communication run alongside. A first look at literature and at Arab culture and civilisation gives you context, and dictionary and study skills teach you to work on your own.

The core stage deepens all of this. Advanced grammar and syntax, advanced morphology and derivation, rhetoric and stylistics (balagha), and prosody and poetic form (arud) are the technical spine. Around them sit classical prose, classical poetry, modern literature, cultural history and identity, and literary criticism. Language-facing core topics are linguistics, dialectology and sociolinguistics, the history of Arabic, translation, teaching Arabic as a second language, media Arabic, lexicography and research methods.

The master’s stage is the scholarly one: the Arabic grammatical tradition, corpus and computational linguistics, advanced theory, and dissertation design.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the script early and never let it slip. Read aloud daily, even ten minutes, because Arabic’s short vowels and case endings are usually not written in ordinary text and are easy to miss in speech. Copy short passages by hand.

Grammar and morphology reward pattern hunting. Learn a root and follow it through its derived forms, then use it in a sentence of your own. Keep a personal vocabulary list with the pattern noted beside each word.

For literature, read the text before the criticism. Note the date, the genre and the main claim of each critic. For every rule or term, write one example you can reproduce in an exam. Check facts about institutions, exam rules and course lengths against your current handbook or official source.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat the dialects and Modern Standard Arabic as one system, then wonder why a sentence sounds wrong. Keep them apart in your notes.

Many learn the letters but not the vowel marks, so they read accurately only when the text is fully marked. Others memorise grammar terms without examples and cannot parse a new sentence.

In literature, a common fault is quoting a critic without knowing when they wrote or what they were arguing against. In translation, word-for-word rendering loses meaning; translate the sense, then check the grammar. In research, avoid claims about a whole language community drawn from a handful of speakers.

keyPoints: Arabic is a Semitic language with a very old written standard that still shapes modern formal writing.
The course joins language skills, linguistics, literature, culture and research.
Degree length, titles and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Keep Modern Standard Arabic and the regional dialects separate in your notes.
Learn grammar and morphology through roots, patterns and your own example sentences.
Read the literary text before the criticism, and date every critic you quote.

en.title: Arabic Script and Phonology
en.short: The Arabic alphabet, letter shapes, vowel signs, sukun, shadda, tanwin, hamza, phonemes and transcription.

sections.heading: Alphabet and joining
sections.text: Arabic is written right to left with 28 letters. It is an abjad: consonants and long vowels are written, but short vowels are usually omitted unless the text is fully vocalised, as in the Qurʼan or grammar examples. Most letters have isolated, initial, medial and final forms. The shape changes with position, but the letter stays the same. Six letters do not join to the following letter: alif, daal, dhaal, raa, zay and waaw. They have only isolated and final forms in normal joining.

sections.heading: Short vowel signs
sections.text: Short vowels use small signs: fatha for a, kasra for i, damma for u. A sukun, a small circle, marks a consonant with no vowel. A shadda doubles a consonant, so it is pronounced twice or held longer. Tanwin is nunation, a final -an, -in or -un, written by doubling the vowel sign; it belongs mainly to formal, fully vocalised Arabic. Hamza is the glottal stop, made by briefly stopping the breath at the throat. It may stand alone or on alif, waaw or yaa. Hamza is not the letter alif.

sections.heading: Sounds and transcription
sections.text: Main consonants include b, t, d, j, k, f, m, n, l, r, s, z, h, w, y, sh, th (as in think), dh (as in this), kh, gh, q, pharyngeal h, ʿayn, and emphatic t, d, s and dh. Exact sounds vary by region. Standard Arabic has short a, i, u; long aa, ii, uu; and diphthongs aw and ay. Long vowels are held longer than short ones. Transliteration into Latin letters varies, so choose one system and keep it consistent. Example: kataba, “he wrote”, is k-a-t-a-b-a. The doubled r in darrasa, “he taught”, shows shadda. Read aloud slowly, check every sign, and compare with a reliable model or teacher.

keyPoints: Arabic has 28 letters and is written right to left; short vowels are usually omitted unless the text is fully vocalised.
Most letters change shape in isolated, initial, medial and final positions; six letters do not join forward.
Fatha, kasra and damma mark short a, i and u; sukun marks no vowel; shadda doubles a consonant; tanwin adds final -an, -in or -un.
Hamza is the glottal stop and is not the same as alif.
Standard Arabic distinguishes short and long vowels, and its consonants include emphatic and pharyngeal sounds that vary by region.
Use one consistent transliteration system; for example kataba is written k-a-t-a-b-a.

en.title: Arabic Morphology: Roots, Patterns and Inflection
en.short: Roots, patterns, noun and verb inflection, and the ten derived verb forms.

sections.heading: Roots and patterns
sections.text:
Arabic words are built from a root, usually three consonants, set into a pattern (wazn). The root carries core meaning; the pattern carries grammar and word class. The model pattern faʿala (فَعَلَ) means "he did".

Put the root k-t-b, about writing, into it: kataba (كَتَبَ), "he wrote". The same root gives kitāb (كِتَاب), "book", kātib (كَاتِب), "writer", and maktab (مَكْتَب), "office" or "desk". Learn roots with patterns, not words alone.

sections.heading: Nouns and inflection
sections.text:
Nouns have gender and inflect for number and case. Gender is masculine or feminine; many feminines end in ta marbuta (ة), but not all. Number is singular, dual (for two) and plural. Plurals are sound, with an ending added, or broken, with a change inside the word, not the root. Case is shown by endings; grammar treats it in detail.

Common patterns include fāʿil for the doer (kātib), mafʿal for a place (maktab), and fiʿāl for many nouns (kitāb). Patterns help you guess meaning.

sections.heading: Verbs and derived forms
sections.text:
Verbs inflect for tense, person, gender and number. Past and present tenses have separate patterns. For k-t-b: past kataba, "he wrote"; present yaktubu (يَكْتُبُ), "he writes". The prefix ya- marks third person masculine singular present.

The ten derived forms add letters to the root and change meaning. Form II often intensifies or makes causative; Form IV often makes causative; Form V is reflexive of II; Form VI is reciprocal of III; Form VII is passive or reflexive; Form VIII is reflexive; Form IX covers colours and defects; Form X means seeking or considering. Learn the forms as a table.

sections.heading: Recognition and production
sections.text:
To recognise a word, remove prefixes and suffixes, find the root, and match the pattern. In kataba al-kātib kitāban, "the writer wrote a book", the root k-t-b appears in all three words.

To produce a form, choose the pattern for the meaning you need. Check a dictionary for broken plurals and irregular forms.

keyPoints: Arabic words are built from a root of usually three consonants set into a pattern.
The root carries core meaning and the pattern carries grammar and word class.
Nouns have gender and inflect for number and case; verbs inflect for tense, person, gender and number.
The ten derived verb forms add letters to the root and change meaning.
To recognise a word, find its root and match its pattern; to produce one, choose the pattern for the meaning.
Learn common patterns such as fāʿil for doer and mafʿal for place.

en.title: Arabic Grammar: Foundations
en.short: Nominal and verbal sentences, case and mood, agreement, pronouns, prepositions and simple parsing.

sections.heading: Nominal and verbal
sections.text: An Arabic sentence is usually nominal (jumla ismiyya) or verbal (jumla fi’liyya). A nominal sentence begins with a noun or pronoun: the topic (mubtada) is nominative, and the predicate (khabar) completes it. The predicate may be a noun, adjective or prepositional phrase. A verbal sentence begins with a verb, then the doer (fa’il), which is nominative, then the object (maf’ul bihi), which is accusative. Word order can change for emphasis, but these roles remain. Example: 'Amina wrote a letter' is parsed as verb, doer, object.

sections.heading: Case and mood
sections.text: Case marks a noun’s grammatical role. The main cases are nominative (raf'), accusative (nasb) and genitive (jarr). A singular noun may show -u, -a and -i endings; dual and sound plural nouns have their own patterns. The present verb has moods: indicative (marfu'), subjunctive (mansub) and jussive (majzum); the imperative is a command form. Particles such as an, lan and lam change mood. Context also matters.

sections.heading: Agreement and pronouns
sections.text: Adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, number, case and definiteness. Verbs agree with the doer in person, gender and number; when the verb comes before its subject, it stays singular. Pronouns are separate (ana 'I', anta 'you', huwa 'he') or attached suffixes that show possession, object or doer. Prepositions govern the genitive, so the noun after a preposition takes genitive case. A basic clause can be topic and predicate, or verb and doer, with an object if the verb takes one. A prepositional phrase can be the predicate.

sections.heading: Parsing simple sentences
sections.text: Parsing (i’rab) means naming each word’s function and its case or mood. First identify the sentence type, then find the verb, doer, object, topic and predicate. Check agreement and prepositions. To produce a correct sentence, choose a pattern, put words in the right case, and match the adjective or verb. For example, in 'the new teacher is in the school', the topic is nominative, the adjective agrees, and the noun after 'in' is genitive.

keyPoints: Arabic sentences are nominal (topic plus predicate) or verbal (verb plus doer plus object).
Nouns show nominative, accusative and genitive case; present verbs show indicative, subjunctive and jussive mood.
Adjectives agree with nouns in gender, number, case and definiteness.
Verbs agree with the doer in person, gender and number; a verb before its subject stays singular.
Prepositions govern the genitive case.
Parsing names each word’s function and case or mood before you produce a sentence.

en.title: Reading and Comprehension
en.short: Graded texts, vocabulary, scanning, inference, context, dictionaries and reading aloud.

sections.heading: Graded reading
sections.text: Graded reading means texts chosen to match your level. Begin with short modern passages on familiar topics, with controlled vocabulary and glosses, which are brief explanations of difficult words. Later texts become longer and less controlled. Classical Arabic prose and poetry may use rare words and long sentences, so read them with a glossary and, where possible, a plain modern explanation. Aim to follow the argument or story, not to know every word.

sections.heading: Building vocabulary
sections.text: Build vocabulary from whole sentences. When you meet a new word, use the context, the words and situation around it, to guess a likely meaning. Then check a dictionary and choose the sense that fits the sentence. Record the word with its sentence. For example, if a text says a traveller missed the bus and reached the examination late, the word for late probably concerns time, not place. Review your list often and read similar texts so words recur.

sections.heading: Main ideas and inference
sections.text: Skimming is a quick read for the main idea, the central point of a paragraph or text. Scanning is a fast search for a detail such as a date, name or number. Inference is a conclusion drawn from clues not stated directly. In an invented case, Amina reads that the bus left at seven and that she reached the hall at half past seven. The text does not say she missed it, but the times support that inference. Check each inference against the text.

sections.heading: Reading aloud
sections.text: Reading aloud joins pronunciation to meaning. Read in short phrases, follow punctuation, and observe printed vowel marks when they appear. If a phrase stops making sense, pause and reread it silently. Do not race. A slow, clear reading that shows understanding is better than a fast reading that ignores meaning. Ask a teacher or a recording to check sounds you cannot yet hear clearly.

keyPoints: Graded texts match your level and grow longer as your reading improves.
Use context first to guess a new word, then check a dictionary and record the word in its sentence.
Skimming gives the main idea; scanning finds a specific detail.
Inference is a conclusion from clues, and every inference should be checked against the text.
Classical Arabic texts often need a glossary and a plain modern explanation.
Reading aloud should join clear pronunciation with understanding, not speed.

en.title: Writing and Composition in Arabic
en.short: Handwriting, spelling, paragraphs, connectors, summaries, formal letters, short essays and editing.

sections.heading: Handwriting and orthography
sections.text:
Handwriting practice in Arabic means forming letters clearly, keeping joins and spaces even, and writing from right to left at a steady size. Orthography is the accepted spelling system: which letters are written, where the glottal stop (hamza) or the feminine ending belongs, and when a letter is pronounced but not written. Learn rules from a trusted dictionary or style guide, and copy short model passages slowly. Check your page for unclear joins and missing dots.

Read your writing aloud after a short pause. You will notice omitted letters and confused endings more easily than while your hand is still moving.

sections.heading: Sentences and paragraphs
sections.text: A sentence needs a subject and a predicate and should express one complete thought. A paragraph develops one main idea. Begin with a topic sentence, add two or three supporting sentences with reasons or examples, and close by linking to the next point. Keep sentences short enough to follow. In an invented case, Amina writes: 'The library opens early. Students use it before lectures. It is quiet, so they can revise.' The sentences share one idea and move in a clear order.

sections.heading: Connectors and summary
sections.text: Connectors are linking words that show addition, contrast, cause, result or sequence. Use them to guide the reader, not to decorate every sentence. A summary restates the main points in fewer words, in your own words, without examples or repetition. Read a passage twice, list its main claims, then write one sentence for each claim. Compare your version with the original to check that no important point is missing and no new claim has been added.

sections.heading: Letters, essays and editing
sections.text: A formal letter has a layout: sender, date, recipient, greeting, subject, body, closing and signature. Layouts vary by country and institution, so check your department’s guide. A short essay has an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. Edit in passes: grammar first, then spelling and orthography, then clarity. Read aloud for flow, and cut sentences that do not support the title.

keyPoints: Handwriting practice aims at clear joins, even spacing and correct dots.
Orthography is the accepted spelling system, so check doubtful words in a dictionary or style guide.
A paragraph should develop one main idea, usually opened by a topic sentence.
Connectors show the relation between ideas and should be used sparingly and accurately.
A summary gives the main points in fewer words and in your own words.
Edit in separate passes for grammar, spelling and clarity, and check formal letter layouts against your institution’s guide.

en.title: Oral Communication in Arabic
en.short: Listening, speaking, pronunciation, conversation, questioning and short presentations in Arabic.

sections.heading: Listening and speaking
sections.text: Oral communication means using speech to understand and be understood. Listening practice trains you to catch main ideas, details, tone and the speaker’s purpose. Speaking practice turns passive knowledge into active use. Work in short, repeated cycles: listen to a short recording, note key words, answer questions, then repeat the content aloud in your own words. Record yourself and compare with a model. This is not about copying an accent; it is about clear, understandable speech.

sections.heading: Pronunciation and fluency
sections.text: Pronunciation practice targets the sounds, stress and rhythm that affect understanding. Arabic has sounds that many learners find hard, and some are distinguished by length or by place of articulation. Practise minimal pairs, words that differ in one sound, and short phrases rather than isolated letters. Fluency grows through repetition and safe mistakes. A useful routine is three minutes of shadowing, where you speak along with a recording, then three minutes of free speech on the same topic.

sections.heading: Conversation and questioning
sections.text: Conversation practice teaches turn-taking, opening and closing, checking understanding and repairing breakdowns. Questioning is a core skill. Closed questions invite yes or no; open questions invite explanation. For example, Amina, a first-year student in Kano, wants to ask a lecturer for an extension. She prepares: greeting, a clear request, a reason, and a polite closing. She avoids a blunt demand and uses a formal register suitable for a lecturer.

sections.heading: Register and presentations
sections.text: Register is the level of formality and the vocabulary suited to a situation. Arabic learners must choose between formal Modern Standard Arabic and the regional spoken variety their listeners use, and must notice when mixing is acceptable. Common difficulties include translating word for word from English, speaking too softly, and preparing a presentation as a written essay. For a two-minute presentation, use one main point, two supporting examples and a clear ending. Rehearse aloud, time it, and invite one question.

keyPoints: Listening and speaking improve through short repeated cycles, not long passive study.
Pronunciation practice should focus on sounds and rhythm that affect understanding.
Conversation needs turn-taking, checking and repair, not only vocabulary.
Open questions invite explanation; closed questions invite yes or no.
Register means choosing formality and variety to suit the listener and situation.
Short presentations work best with one main point, examples and rehearsal aloud.

en.title: Introduction to Arabic Literature
en.short: Genres, periods, oral and written traditions, and key terms for reading Arabic poetry and prose.

sections.heading: Genres and periods
sections.text: Arabic literature is mainly written in Arabic, from the pre-Islamic period through Islamic empires to the modern era. Poetry was long the leading art. The qasida is an ode with a single rhyme throughout; its parts often include a love opening, a journey and praise. Other genres include ghazal (love lyric), madih (praise), hija' (satire), ritha' (elegy) and fakhr (boast); several of these also appear as sections of a qasida. Prose includes khutba (oration), risala (epistle), maqama (episodic rhymed prose) and adab (belles-lettres). The novel and short story belong to the modern period.

sections.heading: Oral and written
sections.text: Early poetry lived in performance and memory. Rawis, professional reciters, transmitted lines before scholars wrote them down. Written prose served courts, administration and religion. Oral and written traditions overlap: a written text may preserve oral style, and an oral performance may use a written script. When studying a text, ask whether it was composed for recitation, for reading, or for both.

sections.heading: Terms for analysis
sections.text: For poetry, a bayt is a line or verse; a diwan is a poet’s collected poems. The matla' is the opening line, qafiya is rhyme, and rawi is the rhyme letter. For prose, khabar is a short report or anecdote, and saj' is rhymed prose. Analysis starts with speaker, addressee, occasion, theme and structure. Then note imagery, repetition and rhyme. Do not impose modern ideas of originality; convention was a shared craft.

sections.heading: A short case
sections.text: Take a qasida opening that names a beloved and an abandoned camp. Ask who speaks, to whom, and what loss is named. Notice how the rhyme holds the line together. Then follow the poem: does it leave the camp for a journey and end in praise of a patron? That movement is a convention, not a rule. A prose khabar can be read similarly: who reports, what changes, and what lesson is drawn?

keyPoints: Arabic literature includes poetry and prose from pre-Islamic times to the modern period.
The qasida is a single-rhyme ode often moving from love opening to journey to praise.
Prose genres include khutba, risala, maqama and adab.
Oral transmission by rawis preserved early poetry before it was written down.
A bayt is a line, a diwan a collection, qafiya rhyme and rawi the rhyme letter.
Analysis asks who speaks, to whom, on what occasion, with what structure and imagery.

en.title: Arabic Culture and Civilisation
en.short: Periods, regions, diversity, art, learning and daily life in Arabic and Islamic civilisation.

sections.heading: Periods and regions
sections.text:
Arabic culture is tied to the spread of Arabic and to Islamic civilisation, but the two are not the same. In the Arabian Peninsula before Islam, oral poetry, trade and tribal life shaped society. From the seventh century CE, Islam and Arabic spread rapidly. The Rashidun, the first four caliphs, ruled from Medina; the Umayyads from Damascus; the Abbasids from Baghdad; the Fatimids from Cairo; and Muslim rule in Andalusia made Cordoba a major centre. Ottoman rule later covered much of the region. European colonialism and modern states reshaped the Arab world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The Arab world is usually described as the Arabic-speaking countries of the Middle East and North Africa. Islamic civilisation is wider: it includes Muslims and non-Muslims, Arabs and non-Arabs, from West Africa to Central Asia.

sections.heading: Diversity
sections.text: Arab and Islamic societies are religiously and ethnically diverse. Muslims form the majority in most Arab countries, but they are not one group: Sunni, Shia and Ibadi traditions differ, and Sufi orders exist within Sunni and Shia Islam. Christians, Jews and other communities have lived in the region for centuries. Ethnic groups include Arabs, Amazigh (Berbers), Kurds, Nubians and Assyrians. Arabic has many dialects, and minority languages such as Berber, Kurdish and Nubian are spoken. So the phrase Arab culture covers many local cultures, not one uniform way of life.

sections.heading: Art, learning, daily life
sections.text:
Islamic art uses calligraphy, geometric patterns and arabesque, a flowing plant-like design. Architecture includes mosques, madrasas (schools), markets and palaces. In learning, the Abbasid translation movement rendered Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and scholars advanced mathematics, medicine and astronomy. Daily life brings these together: a market, a mosque, a school and a family wedding may use Arabic phrases, calligraphy and customs.

Consider Amina, a student in Kano, Nigeria. She speaks Hausa at home, studies Arabic at university and attends a Qur’anic school. At the market she hears Arabic loanwords in Hausa speech and sees Arabic script and calligraphy; at a wedding she hears religious recitation. Her case shows that Arabic culture is both local and global.

keyPoints: Arabic culture and Islamic civilisation overlap but are not identical.
Key periods include the Rashidun, Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Andalusi and Ottoman eras.
The Arab world is mainly the Arabic-speaking Middle East and North Africa, while Islamic civilisation is wider.
Arab and Islamic societies include many religions, ethnic groups and languages.
Calligraphy, geometry, architecture and translation are major cultural achievements.
Daily life in places such as Kano shows Arabic culture as both local and global.

en.title: Dictionary and Study Skills
en.short: Using root-arranged Arabic dictionaries, reference works, transliteration, notes, citation and study planning.

sections.heading: Root dictionaries
sections.text:
Many standard Arabic dictionaries are arranged by root, the consonantal base that carries a word’s core meaning. To find a word, remove prefixes and suffixes, identify the root, then look under it. For example, maktab (office or desk) belongs under the root k-t-b, which relates to writing. Some modern bilingual dictionaries use alphabetical order, so read the guide at the front. Editions differ in page numbers and spelling; note which one you used.

Use the dictionary actively: check the pattern (the template a word is built on, such as maf’al for maktab), plural and part of speech, not only one English gloss. A gloss is a short translation equivalent, and it may fit only some contexts.

sections.heading: Reference works and transliteration
sections.text: Reference works include grammar manuals, literary histories, bibliographies and subject encyclopaedias. Use the library catalogue and ask a subject librarian when unsure. Transliteration is writing Arabic in Latin letters. No single system is universal, so use the one your department requires and apply it consistently. Keep a personal table of letters and marks. When you copy a transliterated word, keep the original Arabic beside it if you can.

sections.heading: Notes and citation
sections.text: Good notes record the Arabic word, its transliteration, root, pattern, meaning, and the source with page number. Citation means giving enough detail for a reader to find the source: author, title, edition, publisher, year, volume and page or entry. Cite dictionary entries by headword or root as well as page. Academic honesty means acknowledging every source, quotation and published translation. Do not present another person’s translation or notes as your own; paraphrase and cite, or quote and cite. Check your department’s policy on collaboration and electronic tools.

sections.heading: Planning study
sections.text: Plan reading and revision for the whole term. Use a weekly timetable with short, frequent sessions, and review notes at spaced intervals. For a language degree, read set texts with a dictionary, keep root-based vocabulary lists, and test yourself by recall rather than rereading. Check the course handbook for deadlines, exam rules and the citation style required.

keyPoints: Many Arabic dictionaries are arranged by root; remove affixes and look under the consonantal root.
Read the dictionary’s introduction because arrangement, edition and spelling conventions vary.
Transliteration writes Arabic in Latin letters; use one department-approved system consistently.
Notes should record word, transliteration, root, pattern, meaning and source page.
Cite author, title, edition, publisher, year, volume and page or entry, including dictionary entries.
Academic honesty requires citing quotations and published translations; plan revision with spaced recall.

en.title: Advanced Arabic Grammar and Syntax
en.short: Complex Arabic sentences: conditionals, exceptions, relatives, particles, case and mood in analysis.

sections.heading: Clause structure
sections.text: Arabic grammar treats a sentence as nominal, beginning with a noun, or verbal, beginning with a verb. A complex sentence has a main clause and one or more subordinate clauses. A subordinate clause may act as a noun, modify a noun, or express a condition. To analyse it, name the head word, the connector and the clause function. In Arabic, a relative clause normally needs a resumptive pronoun, one that refers back to the antecedent, when the relative pronoun is not the subject.

sections.heading: Conditionals and exceptions
sections.text: A conditional sentence has a condition and a result. Arabic conditional particles differ: some govern the jussive mood in both verbs, others do not. Learn each particle with its pattern. Exception uses particles such as illā, meaning 'except'. The case of the excepted noun depends on whether the sentence is affirmative or negative and whether the general noun is mentioned. Analyse the whole sentence, not the particle alone.

sections.heading: Case and mood
sections.text: Case marks nouns and adjectives: nominative for many subjects, accusative for many objects, genitive after prepositions. Mood marks verbs: indicative, subjunctive and jussive. The same Arabic terms may name both case and mood, so state which you mean. Particles and sentence position govern these endings. After a subjunctive particle the verb is subjunctive; after a jussive particle it is jussive. A word’s ending is evidence, not the whole analysis.

sections.heading: Analysing texts
sections.text: When you parse a classical or modern passage, work clause by clause. Mark the sentence type, connectors, relative clauses, conditionals, exceptions, and the case or mood of key words. Then explain how the structure supports the meaning. Classical prose often uses long chains and ellipsis, leaving words understood. Modern prose may use shorter sentences but still depends on particles. For example, in 'When the traveller who had lost his way reached the village, he asked for water', the time clause frames the action, the relative clause identifies the traveller, and 'he' links back.

keyPoints: A complex Arabic sentence has a main clause and subordinate clauses that may act as noun, modifier or condition.
Relative clauses normally need a resumptive pronoun linking back to the antecedent when the relative pronoun is not the subject.
Conditional particles differ in whether they govern the jussive mood, so learn each particle with its own pattern.
In exception with illā, the case of the excepted noun depends on whether the sentence is affirmative or negative and whether the general noun is mentioned.
Case marks nouns and adjectives; mood marks verbs; particles and position govern the endings.
Syntactic analysis names each clause function and explains how structure supports meaning in classical and modern texts.

en.title: Advanced Morphology and Derivation
en.short: Derived verb forms, verbal nouns, participles, plurals, weak verbs and root-pattern analysis.

sections.heading: Roots and patterns
sections.text: Arabic words are built from a root of three consonants, sometimes four, set into patterns called awzān. The root k-t-b carries the idea of writing. Pattern fāʿil gives active participle kātib, one who writes; mafʿūl gives passive participle maktūb, written; fiʿāla gives verbal noun kitāba, writing. A pattern is a template of vowels and affixes; the root fills its consonant slots. This is productive derivation: new words can be formed and understood from a root and pattern.

sections.heading: Derived verb forms
sections.text: The base verb is Form I, with patterns such as faʿala, faʿila and faʿula. Derived forms II to X add consonants, lengthen vowels or add prefixes. Form II faʿʿala is often causative or intensive; III fāʿala reciprocal or transitive; IV ʾafʿala causative; V tafaʿʿala and VI tafāʿala reflexive or reciprocal; VII infaʿala intransitive or passive-like; VIII iftaʿala reflexive or specialised; IX ifʿalla mainly colours and defects; X istafʿala seeking or requesting. Rarer forms XI to XV also exist. Meanings are tendencies, not fixed rules, so check a dictionary.

sections.heading: Nouns and plurals
sections.text: The verbal noun, maṣdar, names the action, as kitāba does for writing. Its patterns are many and learned with the verb. The active participle, ism al-fāʿil, names the doer, kātib; the passive participle, ism al-mafʿūl, names the receiver, maktūb. Derived forms have their own participle patterns, often with a mu- prefix. Plurals are sound or broken. Sound masculine adds -ūn or -īn; sound feminine adds -āt; broken plurals change the pattern, as kitāb becomes kutub. Dictionaries list them.

sections.heading: Weak verbs and analysis
sections.text: Weak roots contain w or y; hollow roots have a weak middle radical, as in q-w-l, qāla, he said. Weak radicals may change or drop, but the pattern still guides recognition. To analyse an unfamiliar word, remove prefixes and suffixes, identify the root consonants, match the pattern, note the form and context, then confirm in a dictionary. For example, istaktaba has prefix ista-, root k-t-b and Form X pattern istafʿala; it means he asked someone to write.

keyPoints: Arabic words are often built from a three- or four-consonant root set into a pattern (wazn).
The common derived verb forms are II to X, with rarer forms XI to XV in classical lists.
Each derived form has tendencies of meaning, not a fixed meaning, so dictionaries are essential.
The verbal noun (maṣdar), active participle (ism al-fāʿil) and passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) are derived nouns with their own patterns.
Plurals are sound (adding -ūn, -īn or -āt) or broken (changing the pattern), and broken plurals are listed in dictionaries.
To analyse an unfamiliar word, strip affixes, find the root, match the pattern, and confirm the meaning in context and in a dictionary.

en.title: Rhetoric and Stylistics in Arabic
en.short: Classical Arabic rhetoric: simile, metaphor, metonymy, concision, emphasis, word order and style analysis.

sections.heading: The rhetorical system
sections.text: Classical Arabic rhetoric, balagha, studies how speech persuades and clarifies. It is usually divided into three branches. Ma’ani treats syntax and word order: how a sentence is built to fit the meaning intended. Bayan treats figures that make meaning clear or vivid: simile, metaphor and metonymy. Badi' treats embellishments such as antithesis and paronomasia (wordplay). The branches overlap. The central test is fit to the situation (muqtada al-hal): the same words may suit one audience and fail another. Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani (d. 1078 CE) argued in Dalail al-I’jaz that eloquence lies in nazm, the arrangement of words in syntax, and in the meanings that arrangement creates.

sections.heading: Figures and meaning
sections.text: A simile (tashbih) compares two things through a shared quality, using a particle such as 'like'. It has four parts: the thing compared, the thing compared to, the shared quality, and the particle. A metaphor (isti’ara) is a simile with one part removed. 'Amina is a lion in the debate' does not say she has fur; it transfers the quality of courage. A metonymy (kinaya) names something literal to imply a related meaning, as 'many ashes’ can imply generosity because many guests were fed. The figure is not decoration. It selects which quality the listener should notice, and it can praise, blame or argue.

sections.heading: Style in practice
sections.text: Concision (ijaz) says much in few words; its opposite, expansion (itnab), may be needed to explain or to move an audience. Emphasis (tawkid) uses repetition, oaths or particles to fix a claim. Word order also carries meaning: in Arabic, a verb-first sentence is the neutral report, while putting the subject first makes it the topic and can suggest emphasis or contrast. To analyse a passage, first paraphrase its plain sense. Then ask which figure is used, what it adds, and why the order or length was chosen. Name the figure only after explaining its work.

keyPoints: Arabic rhetoric (balagha) has three main branches: ma’ani, bayan and badi'.
Simile compares through a shared quality; metaphor drops one part of the comparison; metonymy implies a related meaning.
Al-Jurjani located eloquence in nazm, the syntactic arrangement of words and the meanings it produces.
The central test of style is fit to the situation (muqtada al-hal).
Concision and expansion are choices about how much to say; emphasis is a choice about how strongly to say it.
Word order in Arabic can mark the topic and signal emphasis or contrast, so analyse what a figure adds, not just its name.

en.title: Arabic Prosody and Poetic Form
en.short: Metre, rhyme, scansion, main forms and sound-meaning in Arabic poetry.

sections.heading: Metre and scansion
sections.text: Arabic prosody (ʿarūḍ) studies the sound pattern of poetry. A poem is measured in a metre (baḥr), a repeating sequence of feet. The classical system, traditionally credited to al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, starts from eight basic metres, with derived forms giving around sixteen in all; lists vary. Scansion (taqṭīʿ) marks each letter as moving (mutaḥarrik, vowelled) or quiescent (sākin, unvowelled). These marks form feet (small repeated units) such as faʿūlun. A line (bayt) usually has two hemistichs (ṣadr and ʿajuz).

sections.heading: Rhyme and forms
sections.text: Rhyme (qāfiya) is the recurring sound at the end of lines. Its core is the rawī, the final consonant that stays the same. The qaṣīda is a long poem with one rhyme throughout, often opening with a nasīb (love prelude). The qiṭʿa is a shorter poem on one theme. Andalusian stanza forms such as the muwashshaḥ and zajal use changing rhymes and refrains. Genres include madīḥ (praise), hijāʾ (invective), rithāʾ (elegy) and fakhr (boast).

sections.heading: Sound and meaning
sections.text: Metre is not decoration. A fast, repeated metre can suit narrative or invective; a slow, long metre can suit elegy or solemn praise. Rhyme binds lines and can create closure or surprise. Poets also use alliteration, repetition and vowel colour. Critics disagree about how far sound directly imitates meaning, so treat claims of inherent symbolism with care.

sections.heading: Worked scansion
sections.text: Take the opening of the Mu’allaqa of Imru' al-Qais: qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa-manzil. It is in ṭawīl. Mark the first foot: qi-fā-nab. With / for a moving letter and x for a quiescent one: / / x /. This is faʿūlun, the first foot of ṭawīl. The full metre is faʿūlun mafāʿīlun faʿūlun mafāʿīlun in the first hemistich, and mustafʿilun faʿūlun mafāʿīlun in the second, with allowed variations. Scan the rest by marking every vowelled and quiescent letter, then match the pattern.

keyPoints: Arabic prosody studies metre (baḥr) and scansion (taqṭīʿ) by marking moving and quiescent letters.
A bayt usually has two hemistichs; the classical system recognises around sixteen metres, though lists vary.
Rhyme (qāfiya) centres on the rawī, the final consonant; the qaṣīda is long and monorhymed.
Stanza forms such as the muwashshaḥ and zajal use changing rhymes and refrains.
In ṭawīl, the first foot of qifā nabki is faʿūlun, covering qi-fā-nab and marked / / x /.
Sound can support meaning, but claims of direct imitation need care.

en.title: Classical Arabic Prose: Genres, Authors and Style
en.short: Genres, authors and style of classical Arabic prose, from adab and epistles to history and maqama.

sections.heading: Context and adab
sections.text: Classical Arabic prose grew in a world of tribes, courts, mosques and chanceries. After the Islamic conquests a scribal class served rulers and wrote in a formal register. Adab means literature that educates and entertains, often mixing wisdom, manners and examples. Ibn al-Muqaffa' translated Kalila wa-Dimna, a frame story of animals that teaches statecraft. Al-Jahiz wrote lively essays on animals, rhetoric and society. Courtly prose advised princes and secretaries; didactic prose taught ethics and conduct.

sections.heading: Epistles and oratory
sections.text: A risala is a letter or epistle. Official epistles moved between rulers; literary epistles displayed wit and learning. Al-Jahiz’s epistles are famous for argument and digression. Khutba means public speech or sermon. Pre-Islamic and early Islamic oratory used strong cadence, direct address and moral appeal. A close reading asks who speaks, to whom, and for what purpose. In a sermon repeated phrases build authority; in a court letter balance and allusion show the writer’s skill.

sections.heading: History and narrative
sections.text: Historiography includes annals, dynastic history and biography. Al-Tabari’s universal history arranges reports with chains of transmitters called isnad. Al-Mas’udi wrote topical history and geography. Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddima analyses society and historical method. Narrative prose includes khabar, a report or anecdote, and maqama, a short fictional tale in ornate prose. Badi' al-Zaman al-Hamadhani invented the maqama; al-Hariri perfected it. In al-Hariri’s Maqamat the narrator al-Harith ibn Hammam follows the trickster Abu Zayd al-Saruji. Read one maqama by tracking the frame, the trick and the embedded sermon.

sections.heading: Prose style
sections.text: Style is part of meaning. Saj' is rhymed prose not metre; it marks solemnity or wit. Parallelism, antithesis and quotation of poetry and scripture enrich the text. Historians value a plain chain of authorities; adab writers value surprise and variety. A practical close reading marks repeated sounds, key verbs and shifts in speaker. Then ask how form supports the lesson or the joke. This method works on a letter, a sermon, a history report or a maqama.

keyPoints: Adab is educative and entertaining prose, represented by Ibn al-Muqaffa' and al-Jahiz.
A risala is an epistle; a khutba is a public speech or sermon.
Historiography uses reports and chains of transmitters, as in al-Tabari.
The maqama is a short fictional tale in ornate prose, associated with al-Hamadhani and al-Hariri.
Saj' is rhymed prose, and parallelism and allusion are central prose devices.
Close reading tracks speaker, frame, repetition and the purpose of the passage.

en.title: Classical Arabic Poetry
en.short: Pre-Islamic odes, classical themes, Islamic, Umayyad, Abbasid and Andalusian poetry, and close reading.

sections.heading: Pre-Islamic ode
sections.text: Pre-Islamic poetry (al-shi’r al-jahili) was composed and transmitted orally before Islam and later written down. Its chief form is the qasida, a long monorhyme ode in one metre. The Mu’allaqat preserves famous odes, including Imru' al-Qays’s. A qasida typically moves from a nostalgic amatory prelude (nasib), often at an abandoned campsite, through a desert journey (rahil), to praise (madih), boast (fakhr), satire (hija) or elegy (ritha).

sections.heading: Themes and conventions
sections.text: Pre-Islamic values include muruwwa (manly virtue), hospitality, courage, tribal loyalty and fate. Poetry praises these and attacks rivals. Conventional motifs include the atlal (ruined campsite), the beloved’s departure, the poet’s endurance, and camel or horse descriptions. The speaker often addresses companions or the beloved. Imagery is concrete: desert animals, rain, dust, stars. Sound and repetition matter because poems were performed. A close reading asks who speaks, to whom, at what point in the journey, and how description serves the poem’s purpose.

sections.heading: Islamic and Umayyad
sections.text: After the rise of Islam, poetry continued but changed. Hassan ibn Thabit and others wrote poetry in defence of the Prophet and the community. Some early Muslims distrusted poetry, but it remained central to Arab culture. Under the Umayyads (661-750, Damascus), court and tribal politics produced naqa’id, duelling invective poems exchanged by rival poets. Love poetry flourished: the Hijazi ghazal of Umar ibn Abi Rabi’a is urban and playful, while the Bedouin ghazal of Jamil is chaste and painful.

sections.heading: Abbasid and Andalusian
sections.text: Abbasid poetry, centred in Baghdad from the eighth century, was urban, learned and rhetorically elaborate. Abu Nuwas wrote wine poems (khamriyya) and playful verse; al-Mutanabbi mastered praise and self-assertion; Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi cultivated badi, the display of rhetorical figures. In al-Andalus, poets such as Ibn Zaydun wrote refined love poetry, and strophic forms developed: the muwashshah in classical Arabic and the zajal in colloquial Arabic. Close reading of a selected poem should trace its structure, key images, rhetoric and relation to its patron or beloved.

keyPoints: The qasida is a long monorhyme ode that typically moves from nasib to rahil to a purpose such as praise, boast, satire or elegy.
Pre-Islamic poetry reflects tribal values such as muruwwa, hospitality and loyalty, and uses motifs such as the ruined campsite and the desert journey.
Under Islam and the Umayyads, poetry continued in court and tribal politics, with naqa’id duels and both Hijazi and Bedouin ghazal.
Abbasid poetry became urban and rhetorically elaborate, while Andalusian poetry produced the muwashshah and zajal.
Close reading traces speaker, addressee, structure, imagery, rhetoric and social context rather than only paraphrasing content.

en.title: Modern Arabic Literature: Revival, Genres and Movements
en.short: The nineteenth-century revival, the novel, short story, drama, modern poetry, movements and reading texts.

sections.heading: The nineteenth-century revival
sections.text: The nineteenth-century revival, often called al-nahda, began in the Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire, especially Egypt and Mount Lebanon. Printing, journalism, translation and new schools widened readership. Writers adapted imported genres while keeping Arabic rhetorical traditions. This period prepared the ground for modern literature.

sections.heading: Narrative genres
sections.text: The Arabic novel grew from translations and historical fiction in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It became a major form with social realism, family sagas and experiments in time and voice. Naguib Mahfouz’s Cairo Trilogy is a landmark; he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. The short story flourished in magazines and newspapers, with writers such as Yusuf Idris. Drama developed through Tawfiq al-Hakim and later political theatre. Tayeb Salih’s Season of Migration to the North is a key novel of exile and colonial memory.

sections.heading: Modern poetry
sections.text: Modern Arabic poetry includes the classical qasida, a strict monorhyme ode, and newer free verse (al-shi’r al-hurr) and prose poetry. Poets kept the qasida’s musicality but varied line length and stanza. Badr Shakir al-Sayyab and Nazik al-Malaika are associated with the free-verse movement; Adonis and Mahmoud Darwish extended its possibilities. Themes include exile, city life, politics and myth.

sections.heading: Movements and reading
sections.text: Main movements include romanticism, realism, modernism, postcolonial writing and feminist writing. Recurring themes are identity, colonialism, nationalism, social change, gender, war and displacement. In discussion, read a text closely, then ask how form shapes meaning. For example, compare a chapter of Mahfouz’s Cairo Trilogy with a Darwish poem on exile: note narrative voice, imagery and address. Check translations against the Arabic where possible. Ask also what the text assumes about its audience and about earlier Arabic forms.

keyPoints: The nineteenth-century al-nahda used print, translation, journalism and schools to renew Arabic letters.
The Arabic novel and short story developed in the early twentieth century through translations, historical fiction and social realism.
Naguib Mahfouz’s Cairo Trilogy is a landmark of the Arabic novel, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.
Drama grew through writers such as Tawfiq al-Hakim, while modern poetry adopted free verse and prose poetry.
Main movements include romanticism, realism, modernism, postcolonial and feminist writing.
Recurring themes include identity, colonialism, nationalism, gender, war and displacement; close reading should connect form to meaning.

en.title: Arab Cultural History and Identity
en.short: Arab identity, language and religion, regional diversity, modern debates, music, art and architecture.

sections.heading: Identity formation
sections.text: Arab cultural identity is not a single fixed thing. It grew from tribal and genealogical ties, the prestige of poetry, and shared stories of origin, then was reshaped by Islam, the caliphates, trade and migration. The word Arab has meant different things in different periods: bedouin, speaker of Arabic, or member of a modern nation. Modern Arab nationalism and pan-Arabism, from the late nineteenth century, made language and history central, but nation-states and diasporas produced competing identities. Treat identity as historical, not fixed.

sections.heading: Language and religion
sections.text: Arabic is a Semitic language and the Qur’an is its most influential classical text. This close link gave the language religious prestige and helped standardise grammar and script. But the relation is not simple. Most Muslims are not Arabs, and a significant minority of Arabs are Christian; many are secular. A Muslim from Indonesia may revere Arabic without being Arab; an Arab Christian may pray in Arabic. So language, religion and ethnicity overlap without being identical.

sections.heading: Regional diversity
sections.text: The Arab world stretches from Morocco to Iraq and beyond, and its regions differ in dialect, food, music, law and religious practice. The Maghreb has Amazigh (Berber) heritage; the Levant and Iraq include Kurds, Assyrians and others; the Gulf has Indian Ocean and Iranian links. Such groups are not always Arab, and their presence complicates simple ethnic maps. A concrete case: a Cairene, a Moroccan and a Gulf family may all call themselves Arab, yet their daily language, dress and music differ.

sections.heading: Modern debates and forms
sections.text: Modern debates ask whether Arab identity rests on language, religion, territory or shared struggle. Secularists, Islamists, feminists and diaspora writers disagree. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) criticised Western representations that treated Arabs as exotic or backward; critics now also ask who represents whom inside Arab societies. Music uses maqam scales and rhythmic cycles, art ranges from calligraphy and geometric design to modern painting, and architecture includes courtyard houses, mosques and muqarnas (honeycomb) vaulting. These forms are regional, not uniform, and carry both tradition and critique.

keyPoints: Arab identity is historical and contested, not a fixed essence.
Arabic and Islam are closely linked, but Arabs are not all Muslims and Muslims are not all Arabs.
The Arab world is regionally diverse in language, religion and culture.
Modern debates over secularism, Islamism, feminism and nationalism shape Arab identity.
Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) criticised stereotyped Western representation of Arabs.
Music, art and architecture express regional traditions and modern critical debates.

en.title: Literary Criticism
en.short: Classical and modern Arabic criticism, close reading, evaluation and writing a critical essay.

sections.heading: Classical criticism
sections.text:
Classical Arabic criticism grew from judging poets and poetry. Early critics compared poets, weighed wording (lafz) against meaning (ma’na), and studied the qasida, the formal ode. Al-Amidi’s comparison of Abu Tammam and al-Buhturi is a famous example of evaluative criticism. Critics also asked whether a line was original or borrowed, and how sound and structure supported meaning. These debates were practical: they served reciters, patrons and poets.

This tradition supplies terms still useful today, but it arose in particular social and courtly settings. Use its concepts carefully rather than as timeless rules.

sections.heading: Modern approaches
sections.text:
Modern Arabic criticism borrowed methods from Europe and adapted them. Formalism and structuralism study the text as a system of forms and signs; psychoanalytic criticism reads desire and repression; Marxist criticism asks about class and power; postcolonial criticism examines empire, language and identity; feminist criticism asks how gender shapes writing and reading. Reader-response criticism places meaning in the encounter between text and reader. No single method is final; each reveals some features and hides others.

A good critic states the method being used and its limits. Applying a term such as irony or intertextuality means showing exactly where and how it works in the Arabic text.

sections.heading: Close reading
sections.text:
Close reading begins with the words on the page. Note diction, metaphor, repetition, rhythm, sentence length and shifts in voice. Ask how each choice creates effect. Then connect the passage to its genre and context. For example, in a short modern poem about a city, repeated words for dust and closed doors may build a mood of confinement; check whether the ending confirms or breaks that mood. For a prose passage, ask how narrative voice and sentence rhythm shape judgment. Distinguish description from evaluation.

Evaluation needs criteria: coherence, originality, craftsmanship, emotional force and historical significance. State which criteria you use.

sections.heading: Critical essay
sections.text:
A critical essay makes one arguable claim, the thesis, and supports it with quoted evidence and analysis. Use a clear structure: introduction, body paragraphs, counterargument, conclusion. Quote briefly, translate accurately, and cite editions and page numbers. Evaluate by criteria such as coherence, originality, craftsmanship and historical significance. A useful test: could a careful reader disagree with your thesis? If not, it is summary, not argument.

For Arabic texts, give the original line where possible, then a careful translation. Explain terms such as qasida or maqama, the rhymed-prose narrative, only as needed for your argument.

keyPoints: Classical Arabic criticism evaluated poetry through concepts such as lafz and ma’na and through comparisons of poets.
Modern approaches such as formalism, Marxism, postcolonialism and feminism ask different questions about the same text.
Close reading connects specific word choices and formal features to effects and meaning.
Evaluation should use stated criteria and distinguish description from judgement.
A critical essay needs an arguable thesis supported by quoted evidence and analysis.
Applying critical terms to Arabic poetry and prose requires attention to genre, context and accurate translation.

en.title: Arabic Linguistics: Description and Debate
en.short: Branches of Arabic linguistics, descriptive method, and debates on standard language and variation.

sections.heading: Linguistics as description
sections.text: Linguistics studies language as a system. Applied to Arabic, it asks how sounds, words, sentences and meanings work in actual use. Phonology studies sound units and sound processes; morphology studies word structure; syntax studies phrase and sentence structure; semantics studies literal meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in context. A descriptive analyst records forms and tests patterns with speakers’ judgements, rather than ranking them as good or bad. This is the method behind the debates below.

sections.heading: Sounds and words
sections.text: Phonology distinguishes phonemes, sounds that contrast meaning, from allophones, context-dependent variants of one phoneme. Arabic has processes such as assimilation and vowel shortening, and the analyst must state the environment in which each occurs. Morphology in Arabic often uses a root and pattern system, plus affixes and clitics. A concrete case: kataba (he wrote), kātib (writer), maktab (office) and kitāb (book) share the consonants k-t-b but differ in pattern. The analyst asks which patterns are productive and how speakers form new words.

sections.heading: Sentences and meaning
sections.text: Syntax describes constituency, agreement and word order. Semantics asks about truth conditions, lexical relations such as synonymy, and ambiguity. Pragmatics asks what a speaker implies beyond the literal words, including speech acts (request, apology, promise) and politeness. In Arabic, as in any language, the same sentence can be polite or blunt depending on context, dialect and relationship. The analyst separates what is encoded in the grammar from what is inferred in use.

sections.heading: Standard and variation
sections.text: Prescriptivism sets rules for “correct” usage; descriptivism describes what speakers actually do. Standard Arabic is a codified variety used in formal writing and education in many countries where Arabic is official or taught. Spoken varieties differ by region and situation. This situation is often called diglossia, a stable split between formal and everyday varieties. Linguists debate how much standard norms should shape teaching and media, and how variation should be described without stigma. The choice is social and educational, not settled by linguistics alone.

keyPoints: Linguistics describes Arabic sound, word, sentence and meaning systems rather than judging usage.
Phonology separates phonemes from allophones and states the context of processes such as assimilation.
Arabic morphology often uses root-and-pattern forms, but analysts test productivity with speaker data.
Syntax, semantics and pragmatics study structure, literal meaning and context-dependent meaning.
Prescriptivism sets norms; descriptivism records actual usage; both can inform teaching.
Standard Arabic and spoken varieties differ, and attitudes to variation are social, not purely linguistic.

en.title: Arabic Dialectology and Sociolinguistics
en.short: Regional Arabic dialects, diglossia, registers, code-switching, contact, social variation and attitudes.

sections.heading: Regional dialect groups
sections.text: Arabic dialects form a continuum rather than sharp boxes. Broad labels used in teaching include Gulf, Iraqi, Levantine, Egyptian, Maghrebi, Yemeni and Sudanese. Each label hides local variation, and Bedouin and sedentary speech may differ within one country. Mutual intelligibility is often partial: speakers of distant dialects may need to shift towards a common form. The standard written language, Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), is not a mother tongue in the usual sense.

sections.heading: Diglossia and register
sections.text: Diglossia, as described by Charles Ferguson in 1959, is a stable division between a high variety used in writing, education and formal speech and a low variety used in everyday talk. Arabic is a classic example, but the picture is more complex. Badawi described levels between MSA and colloquial Egyptian, and educated spoken Arabic mixes formal and dialect features. Register means the variety chosen for a situation, such as a lecture, a radio interview or a market conversation. Speakers often move along a scale rather than choose one fixed code.

sections.heading: Code-switching and contact
sections.text: Code-switching is moving between varieties or languages within a conversation or sentence. In Arabic it may mean switching between MSA and a dialect, or between Arabic and French, English or another contact language. Language contact has left loanwords and structures in many dialects, for example French in Maghrebi and English in Gulf speech. Contact does not simply replace Arabic; it reshapes it. A Cairo student may write an essay in MSA, chat in Egyptian Arabic, and use an English technical term.

sections.heading: Social variation and attitudes
sections.text: Social variation follows age, gender, education, class, region and urban or rural life. Migration and media can cause dialect levelling, the loss of local features in favour of wider forms. Attitudes matter: standard Arabic often carries prestige as the language of religion, literature and formal education, while dialects carry intimacy and local identity. Yet a dialect may be stigmatised in school or employment. These judgements are social, not linguistic, and they vary by country and community.

keyPoints: Arabic dialects form regional continua, not sharp boundaries; broad groups include Gulf, Iraqi, Levantine, Egyptian, Maghrebi, Yemeni and Sudanese.
Diglossia is the stable use of a high variety for formal functions and a low variety for everyday talk.
Register is the variety chosen for a situation, and educated spoken Arabic often mixes standard and dialect features.
Code-switching is moving between MSA, a dialect or another language within talk.
Language contact leaves loanwords and structures but does not simply replace Arabic.
Attitudes to standard Arabic and dialects are social judgements about prestige and identity, and they vary by community.

en.title: History of the Arabic Language
en.short: From pre-Islamic Arabic to the classical standard, loanwords, script and modern language academies.

sections.heading: Origins and Quran
sections.text: Arabic is a Semitic language. Its early forms are known from inscriptions, from pre-Islamic poetry transmitted orally, and from the Quran, revealed in the seventh century CE. The Quran became the central model of classical Arabic, the standard used in writing and formal speech. Early grammarians in Basra and Kufa described this usage, drawing on poetry, the Quran and Bedouin speech. Their work fixed a prestige norm, but it did not stop change in everyday speech.

sections.heading: Standard and borrowing
sections.text: Classical Arabic spread with Islam and administration. As it met Greek, Persian, Aramaic and later European learning, it borrowed words and adapted them to Arabic patterns. The Greek philosophia became falsafa, and English algebra and alcohol come from Arabic. Borrowing was not simple copying: speakers reshaped sounds and forms. At the same time Arabic supplied many technical terms to other languages. Purists often preferred derivation from Arabic roots, while users accepted useful loans.

sections.heading: Script and academies
sections.text: The Arabic script developed from earlier Semitic writing; the exact route is debated. Early manuscripts lack full vowel marks, so diacritics were added to protect Quranic reading. In the modern period, print, schools, journalism and translation created new vocabulary. Language academies, especially in Cairo, Damascus, Baghdad and Rabat, coin terms and publish decisions. They usually favour derivation and analogy over direct borrowing. Their choices influence education and media, but ordinary usage can ignore them.

sections.heading: Evidence and change
sections.text: Language history rests on inscriptions, papyri, manuscripts, poetry and comparison with other Semitic languages. Each source has limits. Inscriptions are short, and poetry was written down after oral transmission. Scholars debate how uniform early Arabic was and when the script reached its present form. Modern standard Arabic is used in writing and formal speech, while regional spoken varieties differ. This situation, called diglossia, is central to debates about change, reform and identity.

keyPoints: Arabic is a Semitic language whose classical norm was shaped by the Quran, early poetry and the work of grammarians in Basra and Kufa.
Classical Arabic borrowed and adapted words from Greek, Persian, Aramaic and European languages, and Arabic itself supplied terms to other languages.
The Arabic script developed from earlier Semitic writing, though the exact route is debated; diacritics were added to protect Quranic reading.
Modern language academies in Cairo, Damascus, Baghdad and Rabat coin terms, usually preferring derivation and analogy to direct borrowing.
Modern Standard Arabic is used in writing and formal speech, while regional spoken varieties differ, a situation called diglossia.
Evidence for language history comes from inscriptions, papyri, manuscripts, poetry and comparative Semitic study, and each source has limits.

en.title: Translation between Arabic and English
en.short: Covers equivalence, register, cultural and religious terms, ethics, practical Arabic-English translation and revision.

sections.heading: Equivalence and brief
sections.text:
Translation produces a target text for a reader and a purpose. Equivalence is the relation between source and target. Formal equivalence stays close to source wording and structure. Dynamic equivalence, which Nida later called functional equivalence, aims at the same effect on the reader. Eugene Nida set out this pair in the 1960s. No method is always right.

Skopos theory, linked to Vermeer and Reiss, says the brief decides. A legal contract may need formal equivalence to show every obligation. A tourist leaflet may need dynamic equivalence to read naturally. The brief states audience, purpose, register and deadline.

sections.heading: Register and culture
sections.text:
Register is the variety of language chosen for a situation. Michael Halliday describes it through field (topic), tenor (relationship between writer and reader) and mode (spoken or written). Arabic formal prose often uses long sentences and repetition; English academic prose often prefers shorter sentences and explicit links. The translator adjusts without changing the message.

Cultural and religious terms rarely have exact equivalents. Hajj, the pilgrimage to Makkah, and zakat, obligatory almsgiving, are examples. A translator may keep the term and add a short gloss, or use a descriptive phrase. Respect and accuracy matter. Avoid a word that misleads, and explain a term on first use.

sections.heading: Practice, revision, ethics
sections.text:
Use a translation brief. Draft, leave it, then revise against the source. Check names, dates, figures and negations. Back-translation, putting the target back into the source language, can reveal gaps, but it is only a check.

Case: a Kano university sends a transcript to a United Kingdom university. The translator keeps course titles and grades, adds a glossary note for local terms, and does not convert marks without the official scale. A second reader checks it.

Ethics means competence, confidentiality, accuracy and impartiality. Accept only work you can do well. Keep client information private. Do not invent facts or soften a statement without permission. Disclose conflicts of interest and correct errors openly. In legal or medical settings, follow the rules of the country concerned.

keyPoints: Equivalence is a relation between source and target, not a word-for-word rule.
Formal equivalence follows source form; dynamic equivalence aims at the same effect.
The translation brief sets audience, purpose, register and deadline.
Register covers field, tenor and mode, and the translator adjusts style without changing meaning.
Cultural and religious terms often need a gloss or description rather than a false equivalent.
Ethics require competence, confidentiality, accuracy, impartiality and open correction of errors.

en.title: Teaching Arabic as a Second or Foreign Language
en.short: Methods, materials, syllabus, assessment, errors and lesson planning for teaching Arabic as a foreign language.
keywords: teaching Arabic as a foreign language

sections.heading: Needs and goals
sections.text: Start with a needs analysis: find out why learners study Arabic, their prior knowledge, literacy in Arabic script, exposure to spoken varieties, and time. A beginner who wants to read the Quran, a heritage speaker who understands a dialect at home, and a student preparing to study in Cairo have different goals. Decide early which variety or varieties to teach. Modern Standard Arabic is the usual base for reading and formal writing, while a spoken variety may be needed for everyday talk. Say what the course will and will not cover.

sections.heading: Methods and materials
sections.text: Grammar-translation teaches rules and translation, often with reading. Audio-lingual methods use drills and repetition. Communicative language teaching puts meaningful interaction first, and task-based learning asks learners to complete a real task, such as planning a trip, in the target language. Most modern courses mix approaches. Materials may be a textbook, authentic texts made for real readers, audio, video and teacher-made dialogues. Choose materials that match the goal, level and variety, and check that examples are accurate.

sections.heading: Syllabus and lesson
sections.text: A syllabus states objectives, content, sequence and assessment. It can be organised by grammar, functions such as greeting and requesting, situations, or tasks. A short lesson plan should state the level, objective, materials and timing. For example, a 45-minute intermediate lesson on asking for directions might use: warm-up 5 minutes, presentation 10, controlled practice 10, role-play 15, feedback 5. The total is 45 minutes. Include a check that learners can do the task without help.

sections.heading: Assessment and errors
sections.text: Placement tests decide the starting level. Diagnostic assessment finds gaps. Formative assessment, such as quizzes and observation, guides teaching; summative assessment grades achievement at the end. Test what was taught and use clear rubrics. In error analysis, collect learner language, classify errors, and separate systematic errors from slips. Interlanguage is the learner’s developing rule system. Fossilisation is an error that has become fixed. Give feedback that fits the aim: correction for accuracy work, and delayed feedback for fluency tasks.

keyPoints: Needs analysis should record goals, prior Arabic, script literacy, the variety needed and time available.
Communicative and task-based methods prioritise meaningful use, while grammar-translation and audio-lingual methods focus on rules and drills.
A syllabus can be sequenced by grammar, functions, situations or tasks.
A lesson plan states objective, level, materials, stages and timing, and checks whether learners can do the task.
Placement, diagnostic, formative and summative assessment serve different purposes.
Error analysis separates systematic errors from slips and plans feedback; interlanguage is the learner’s developing system.

en.title: Arabic Media and Contemporary Texts
en.short: Reading and analysing Arabic news, broadcast and online texts, with summary and comment.

sections.heading: Media Arabic
sections.text: Media Arabic is the register of newspapers, television news and news websites. It is mostly Modern Standard Arabic, the formal variety shared across the Arab world, though interviews may include dialect. Learn fields: politics, security, economy, health and sport. Notice set phrases, official titles, abbreviations and loanwords. A news item answers who, what, when, where, why and how early. Headlines compress this and omit helping words, so read the lead, the first sentence, to recover the full claim.

sections.heading: Reading news
sections.text: Read a report in layers. First identify source, date and genre: news report, feature, editorial or social media post. Then mark the main actor, action, object, place and time. Separate fact from claim and opinion. Check numbers and dates against the text. In a hypothetical example, a headline says Council approves 300 new houses; the lead must say which council, when, and whether 300 were built or planned. If 120 are for rent, then 120 ÷ 300 = 40% are rental units.

sections.heading: Framing and bias
sections.text: Framing is the choice of angle, words and images that makes one aspect of a story stand out. Agenda setting is the power to decide which issues receive attention. Gatekeeping is the selection of what enters publication. Compare outlets: note active or passive voice, labels, metaphors, quoted sources and omitted voices. A protest can be called a sit-in by one outlet and unrest by another; both can be accurate, but each directs attention differently. Ask who benefits and what evidence is missing.

sections.heading: Summarising and comment
sections.text: A summary states the central claim and main supporting facts in neutral words, without copying the outlet’s tone. Use a short frame: source, event, actors, claim, evidence, context. For comment, judge accuracy, balance and relevance. Distinguish reported fact from inference. Add background from reliable sources, and say clearly when you give your own view. In broadcast and online texts, check timestamps and updates, because stories change after publication.

keyPoints: Media Arabic is mostly Modern Standard Arabic, with dialect mainly in interviews and social posts.
Read a news text in layers: source and genre, then actor, action, time, place, claim and evidence.
Separate reported fact from claim, opinion and inference before summarising.
Framing, agenda setting and gatekeeping shape which facts and voices stand out.
A summary should be neutral and short; a comment should judge accuracy, balance and relevance and declare the writer’s view.
Check timestamps and updates in broadcast and online texts because stories change.

en.title: Arabic Lexicography: Dictionaries and Their Entries
en.short: Root order, classical and modern Arabic dictionaries, usage labels and comparing entries.

sections.heading: Roots and arrangement
sections.text: Arabic dictionaries are built on roots. A root is usually three consonants, such as k-t-b, and words are filed under it: kataba, kitāb, kātib and maktab sit together. Two orders are common. The rhyme order (tartīb al-qawāfī) files roots by their last letter, so k-t-b goes under b. The alphabetical order files by the first letter, so k-t-b goes under k. Most modern dictionaries use the alphabetical order, which suits learners.

sections.heading: Classical and modern works
sections.text: Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad’s Kitāb al-ʿAyn, from the eighth century CE, used a phonetic order based on where a letter is pronounced. Al-Jawharī’s al-Ṣiḥāḥ, Ibn Manẓūr’s Lisān al-ʿArab and al-Fīrūzābādī’s al-Qāmūs al-Muḥīṭ use the rhyme order; al-Zabīdī’s Tāj al-ʿArūs builds on them. Historical dictionaries quote dated sources and trace senses over time. Modern works include al-Muʿjam al-Wasīṭ of the Arabic Language Academy in Cairo, and the large historical project al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr. For English readers, Lane’s Arabic-English Lexicon and Wehr’s Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic are standard.

sections.heading: Reading an entry
sections.text: An entry usually gives the headword with its vowels, the root, the grammatical class and the plural. Senses are numbered. Usage labels warn the reader: classical or modern, rare, obsolete, colloquial, figurative, technical. Examples, often a verse or a hadith, show the word in use. Check the label before you use a word, because a sense marked rare may puzzle a listener.

sections.heading: Comparing entries
sections.text: Take hātif. Classical dictionaries record it as a voice heard when the speaker is not seen. Modern Arabic uses it for telephone, and modern dictionaries record that sense. Comparing the two shows a dictionary fixing one moment in the language. When you compare entries, note the order of senses, the labels and the examples, and ask which sense is placed first, since that choice guides the reader.

keyPoints: Arabic dictionaries file words under a root of usually three consonants.
Classical dictionaries such as al-Ṣiḥāḥ and Lisān al-ʿArab use the rhyme order, filing roots by their last letter.
Most modern dictionaries file roots by their first letter.
Usage labels mark a sense as classical, modern, rare, colloquial or figurative, and readers should check them.
Historical dictionaries quote dated sources and trace senses over time.
Comparing entries for one word, such as hātif, shows how dictionaries record change.

en.title: Research Methods in Arabic Studies
en.short: Framing questions, evaluating sources, textual and qualitative methods, citation and research proposals.

sections.heading: Asking a question
sections.text: A research question states what you will find out, not what you already believe. It should be narrow enough for a small project and answerable with available sources. Turn a topic into a question: not “Arabic novels and migration” but “How does one contemporary Arabic novel present a migrant’s return home?” Define key terms and set limits of time, place and texts. A good question guides the sources you need and the method you choose.

sections.heading: Finding sources
sections.text: Primary sources are the texts or people you study: a novel, poem, manuscript, interview or recording. Secondary sources are studies about them. Search library catalogues and subject databases, then evaluate each item by author, publisher, date, evidence and purpose. Prefer peer-reviewed work, meaning studies checked by other scholars before publication, but use older scholarship with care. Keep a search log. For a project on an Arabic novel in translation, compare the Arabic text with the translation and read reviews of both.

sections.heading: Textual and qualitative methods
