sections.text: Textual method means close reading: describe the text, note patterns, compare editions or translations, and support every claim with quotation or page reference. Qualitative method collects words or observations, not numbers. Interviews need consent, safe storage and anonymity. Label responses by theme. Case: Amina, a student in Kano, asks how five readers in a book club discuss an Arabic novel. She records consent, transcribes interviews, groups comments by theme and checks her reading against the text.

sections.heading: Citation and proposal
sections.text: Citation records the source of every idea, quotation and paraphrase, so readers can find it and you avoid plagiarism. Use one style consistently, such as Chicago or APA, and follow your department’s guide. A short proposal usually states the title, question, aims, a brief literature review of what has already been written on the question, method, sources, ethics and timetable. Plan a realistic scope. Check spelling of names and titles, and keep full bibliographic details from the first reading.

keyPoints: A research question is narrow, answerable and states what you will find out.
Primary sources are the texts or people studied; secondary sources are studies about them.
Evaluate sources by author, publisher, date, evidence and purpose.
Textual method uses close reading and page references; qualitative method labels interviews or observations by theme.
Cite every quotation and paraphrase in one consistent style.
A short proposal states question, aims, literature, method, sources, ethics and timetable.

en.title: The Arabic Grammatical Tradition: Formation, Method and Legacy
en.short: How Arabic grammar formed, its methods and debates, and its links to modern linguistics.

sections.heading: Formation and schools
sections.text: Arabic grammar, nahw, grew from concern to preserve correct recitation of the Qur’an and understanding of early poetry. Scholars gathered usage from attested Arabic speech, the Qur’an and poetry. Basra and Kufa became centres. Sibawayh’s al-Kitab, the earliest surviving comprehensive grammar, set a model: describe forms, then explain them by rules. The Basran and Kufan schools disagreed on method and details, but the split was not absolute; later works record their disputes.

sections.heading: Methods and concepts
sections.text: Grammarians used sama', attested usage, and qiyas, analogy from attested forms to new cases. An 'illa, cause or explanatory principle, justified a rule. I’rab, case and mood marking, shows syntactic role. The theory of 'amal, government, says an operator such as a verb or particle assigns case or mood to a dependent word. Example: in kataba Zaydun al-kitaba, Zayd wrote the book, Zaydun is nominative as subject and al-kitaba accusative as object. Such examples show how rules connect form to function.

sections.heading: Debates and texts
sections.text: Debates concerned the weight of transmitted usage against analogy, the reality of causes, and the status of rare forms. The Basrans are often seen as stricter in analogy; the Kufans as more willing to accept transmitted oddities. Ibn Jinni’s al-Khasa’is discusses language as convention and the limits of analogy. Ibn al-Anbari’s al-Insaf sets out Basran and Kufan arguments on disputed questions. Read passages in translation with care: translations differ, and technical terms rarely map one-to-one onto English.

sections.heading: Modern theory
sections.text: Modern linguists treat the tradition as a sophisticated descriptive grammar of classical Arabic, though it also became normative. Its rule-and-exception method resembles later structural description, and 'amal has been compared with dependency grammar, but the comparison is partial. The tradition focused on a prestige variety and written texts; modern sociolinguistics studies dialects and speech. Reading the texts in translation helps students see both the achievements and the assumptions of the tradition.

keyPoints: Arabic grammar grew from Qur’anic recitation, poetry and attested usage, with Basra and Kufa as early centres.
Sibawayh’s al-Kitab is the earliest surviving comprehensive Arabic grammar and a model for later works.
Grammarians combined sama', attested usage, with qiyas, analogy, and sought 'illa, explanatory causes.
I’rab marks case and mood, while 'amal theory explains how operators govern dependent words.
Basran and Kufan disputes, recorded in Ibn al-Anbari’s al-Insaf, concerned method and particular rules.
The tradition is a major descriptive grammar, but comparisons with modern linguistic theories must be made cautiously.

en.title: Arabic Corpus and Computational Linguistics
en.short: The summary covers Arabic corpora, annotation, morphology, encoding, machine translation, limits and study design.

sections.heading: Corpora and encoding
sections.text: A corpus is a structured, machine-readable collection of texts chosen for a purpose. Arabic corpora vary: Modern Standard Arabic news, classical texts, dialects and speech transcripts. Size and balance affect the claims you can make. Store Arabic in Unicode, usually UTF-8; normalise optional diacritics, tatweel and alef forms; handle right-to-left display. Buckwalter transliteration maps Arabic letters to ASCII for tools. Do not strip diacritics blindly if meaning depends on them.

sections.heading: Annotation and morphology
sections.text: Annotation adds labels: part of speech, lemma, root, clitics, syntax and named entities. Guidelines and double annotation with inter-annotator agreement, a measure of how far annotators agree, are needed. Schemes differ, so compare labels carefully. Arabic morphology is rich: one word can carry prefixes, stem and suffixes; root-and-pattern analysis; clitics; ambiguity. A morphological analyser returns possible analyses; disambiguation needs context. Diacritics are often absent, increasing ambiguity.

sections.heading: Applications and limits
sections.text: Applications include machine translation, information retrieval, sentiment, named entity recognition, optical character recognition (OCR), speech and dialect identification. Other uses include question answering and author profiling. Arabic machine translation is hard because of morphology, dialect, orthography and scarce parallel data for dialects. Evaluation uses BLEU, a score based on matching word sequences with a reference translation, but BLEU is only a rough proxy; human judgement and error analysis matter. Limits include licence, domain, dialect imbalance, annotation quality and benchmark overfitting.

sections.heading: Small study design
sections.text: Small study: state the question, choose a corpus and licence, split train/dev/test, set a baseline, choose metrics, do error analysis, and make it reproducible. Use a held-out test set; report raw counts as well as scores. Example: on 500 tokens, gold has 300 root-bearing tokens. The system marks 280 as root; 240 are correct. Precision is 240 ÷ 280 = 85.7%; recall is 240 ÷ 300 = 80%; F1 is 2 × 240 ÷ (2 × 240 + 40 + 60) = 480 ÷ 580 = 82.8%. Report limits.

keyPoints: A corpus is a structured, machine-readable text collection; its design and licence limit what you can claim.
Arabic corpora need careful Unicode handling and normalisation of optional diacritics, tatweel and alef forms.
Annotation adds labels such as part of speech, lemma, root and syntax; guidelines and inter-annotator agreement measure quality.
Arabic morphology is rich and ambiguous, so analysers return multiple analyses and need context to disambiguate.
Machine translation and other applications are limited by morphology, dialect, orthography, parallel data and evaluation proxies such as BLEU.
For a small study, use a held-out test set and report precision, recall and F1 with raw counts; F1 = 2TP ÷ (2TP + FP + FN).

en.title: Advanced Literary and Cultural Theory
en.short: Key theory for reading Arabic texts: identity, power, gender, postcoloniality and reception.

sections.heading: Theory as method
sections.text:
Theory is a set of concepts that helps you ask better questions of a text. A theoretically informed argument states a claim, defines its terms, reads close evidence, and answers a likely objection. Do not use theory as decoration. Ask what a concept lets you see in the Arabic text that a plain reading misses.

Michel Foucault treats power as spread through discourse, the language and institutions that make some statements speakable. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) argues that Western writing often produced the East as an object of knowledge and control. Use such ideas to examine who speaks, who is represented, and for whom.

sections.heading: Identity and postcoloniality
sections.text:
Postcolonial theory studies the effects of colonial rule and the ways texts resist, imitate or complicate it. Homi Bhabha’s hybridity names the mixed, unstable identities that colonial contact produces. Gayatri Spivak’s "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) asks whether the most marginalised can be represented without being spoken for.

A concrete case is Tayeb Salih’s novel Season of Migration to the North (Arabic 1966). A postcolonial reading can ask how the narrator’s return to Sudan and his encounter with the story of Mustafa Sa’eed expose colonial desire, mimicry (imitating the coloniser, almost the same but not quite) and unresolved history. Keep the argument tied to passages, not to a general claim that the novel shows colonialism.

sections.heading: Gender and reception
sections.text:
Gender theory asks how texts construct masculinity, femininity and desire, and how readers are positioned. Judith Butler’s Gender Trouble (1990) argues that gender is performed through repeated acts rather than expressed from an inner essence. Apply this carefully to Arabic texts: ask what norms a text repeats, what it destabilises, and what it silences.

Reception theory, associated with Hans Robert Jauss and Wolfgang Iser, studies how readers and communities make meaning. A text’s reception changes with time, translation and audience. For an Arabic work, compare its first readers, later critics, and English translation’s readers. That comparison can become your argument about power and value.

keyPoints: A theoretically informed argument uses concepts to ask precise questions, not to decorate a reading.
Foucault links power to discourse, and Said’s Orientalism shows how knowledge can represent and control the East.
Postcolonial theory examines colonial effects; Bhabha’s hybridity and Spivak’s subaltern question identity and voice.
Gender theory, as in Butler, treats gender as performed and asks what norms a text repeats or unsettles.
Reception theory studies how different readers and periods make meaning from a text.
Tie every theoretical claim to specific passages, context and likely objections.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation Design
en.short: Research questions, literature review, textual and empirical methods, ethics, proposal design and defence.

sections.heading: From question to plan
sections.text: A master’s dissertation begins with a research question that is narrow enough to answer within the time and resources available. The question should name a problem, a gap in existing work, and the evidence you will use. A proposal turns this into a plan: title, background, aims, question, literature review, method, sources, timetable, ethics and bibliography. Keep the scope realistic. An invented example: Amina studies how Arabic loanwords are used in Hausa radio news in Kano. She limits herself to one station and three months of broadcasts.

sections.heading: Reading the field
sections.text: A literature review is not a list of summaries. It groups studies by question and method, shows where they agree or disagree, and identifies the gap your work addresses. Use primary and secondary sources, and record full bibliographic details as you read. For textual work, ask which edition or manuscript you use and why. For empirical work, ask whether your sample and instruments can answer the question.

sections.heading: Methods and ethics
sections.text: Textual approaches analyse texts, editions, language or arguments closely. Empirical approaches collect data through interviews, observation, questionnaires or recorded speech. Mixed methods combine both. Ethics require informed consent, anonymity where promised, secure data storage, honest citation and permission for private or copyrighted material. Most universities require ethics review before data collection. Check your institution’s rules.

sections.heading: Proposal and defence
sections.text: A strong proposal states the question, why it matters, what has been done, what you will do, and how you will do it. Present the plan in a short talk: problem, gap, method, timetable and limits. In the defence, answer questions directly. If you do not know, say so and explain how you will find out. Revise the plan after feedback.

keyPoints: A master’s dissertation question must be narrow, answerable and linked to a gap in existing work.
A literature review groups studies by question and method and identifies the gap, rather than listing summaries.
Textual methods analyse texts and editions; empirical methods collect data; mixed methods combine both.
Ethics require informed consent, anonymity, secure data, honest citation and permission, and usually ethics review.
A proposal states the question, gap, method, timetable, ethics and limits.
In a defence, answer directly, admit uncertainty, and revise the plan after feedback.
